newsitem.title: UK: PRESS DIGEST - Financial Times - June 16 1997.
newsitem.headline: PRESS DIGEST - Financial Times - June 16 1997.

text.p: This daily press summary is produced for Reuters by the Broadcast Monitoring Company, which is responsible for its contents. -- BROWN MAY SCRAP DIVIDEND CREDIT

The UK Treasury is considering abolishing the 20 percent tax credit on dividend payments, a move that could raise up to five billion sterling from pension funds and other tax-exempt institutions. The cuts would come as part of next month's budget, which will not include the end to mortgage tax relief or other big changes to personal tax, as Tony Blair has indicated he will retain his manifesto pledge not to raise the basic or top rates of income tax.
-- NORWICH UNION SET FOR BUOYANT DEBUT

Norwich Union shares are expected to make an impressive stock market debut on Monday at well above the 290p price confirmed for the public offer. The flotation will make Norwich Union, at 5.6bn stg, the UK's third largest quoted insurer behind Prudential and Royal & Sun Alliance. The majority of the 2.9 million NU members receiving free shares will have a chance to purchase further shares with a 25p discount.
-- AIRBUS CHIEF HITS OUT AT MCDONNELL DOUGLAS

Airbus Industrie managing director Jean Pierson has accused McDonnell Douglas of 'throwing away' the opportunity to win the US Joint Strike Fighter project in an attempt to ease the company's planned merger with Boeing. Pierson claims that McDonnell deliberately failed to meet government specifications when bidding on the project, whose final bidders are now Boeing and Lockheed Martin. Airbus has referred to the merger between the Boeing and McDonnell Douglas an attempt to 'financially throttle' Airbus.
-- SIB MAY BE URGED TO LET CITY BREATHE

The UK government is expected to encourage the new Securities and Investments Board to be more lenient in the way it regulates banks and securities brokers. Officials have expressed concern that the SIB may be over cautious and seek to stifle legitimate financial risk-taking due to the growing political and public pressure on the Bank of England in prominent cases of banking scandals and collapses. The current UK Banking Act does not include any explanation of the principles underlying regulation.
-- COMMISSIONER HOPEFUL OF SWIFT FISHERIES DEAL

European transport commissioner Neil Kinnock has said he is 'certain' that progress will be made at an Amsterdam summit on fisheries quota-hopping after almost a month of talks between Britain and other affected companies. Any deal made would not outlaw the practice of foreign boats operating under British licenses, but would require Spanish fishermen to establish closer economic links with EU communities, employ one or more British fisherman and comply with British safety rules.
-- EX-EXECUTIVE WARNS ON COAL INDUSTRY DECLINE

A study on the state of the British coal industry by energy consultancy Oxera indicates that the industry is in a state of terminal decline and the rate of measures introduced to revive the industry do not seem feasible. Malcolm Edwards of Oxera claims that coal-mining company RJB's 'vigorous stance' on price and tonnage with the electricity generators has encouraged the generators to establish al ternative sources of supply, including searches abroad. Other reasons given for the decline include the interaction of privatisation, increased use of gas by UK generators, environmental constraints and low costs for imported coal.
-- TESCO PLANS CREDIT TEST TERMINALS

Supermarket group Tesco has set up Tesco Personal Finance, a joint venture between it and Royal Bank of Scotland offering financial products such as mortgages and general and life insurance. Terminals will be set up in Tesco stores to allow shoppers to test their credit rating so the company can avoid offending customers by rejecting applications for loans and mortgages. TPF chie f executive Derek Sach revealed that if the company can 'find a way to encourage people not to apply for things they won't get, that could help us ensure they remain contented customers for Tesco'.
-- GAS PRICE BATTLE NEARS END

Ofgas director general Clare Spottiswoode will this week publish findings of an Monopolies and Mergers Commissions study aimed at resolving the ongoing battle over charges for use of the UK gas transmission system, a study industry executives believe is set to end in a 'messy fudge'. The executives believe no clear-cut victory will be given to either side, nor will any regulatory certainty be given to BG.
-- COMPUTER GROUPS AIM TO BRING PC TECHNOLOGY TO TV

Intel, Compaq and Microsoft have joined forces to form the DTV group, in a campaign to persuade the European television industry it needs PC technology for its development. DTV is based on the platform that PC technology can ultimately deliver better quality pictures for television and an additional audience for programmers. The DTV group has detailed its ideas to the National Association of Broadcasters conference in the US.
-- MANNESMANN PLANS DUAL-USE PHONE SYSTEM

German industrial giant Mannesmann has announced plans to develop Europe's first mass-market digital telephone service, which would allow customers to use a single phone as both a cordless telephone at home and as a mobile elsewhere. Over the next five years, Mannesmann will invest between 1.05bn stg and 1.41bn stg in telecommunications, highlighting the change in the German market, which will become liberalised in January.
